paras: The lynching of George Porter was the killing of a man by a mob in Lampasas County, Texas, on the night of August 2, 1882. About twenty-five men took Porter from a cattleman's camp and shot him to death because he was suspected of horse stealing. The killing was reported in a Lampasas letter to the Dallas Herald and then spread as a one-sentence wire item to papers in several states.

Porter was at the camp of J. P. Higgins, described as "a cattle man" in Lampasas County. According to the Lampasas correspondent, he "had a stolen horse in his possession," while the wire version said only that the horse was "supposed to be stolen." None of the reports gives Porter's race, age or background.

On Wednesday night, a mob of about twenty-five men went to Higgins's camp and "took out" Porter. They shot him several times, "riddling him with bullets." The wire account added that his body was left on the roadside near Lampasas.
The coverage does not name any member of the mob, and no report of an inquest, arrest or grand jury action was found.

The Dallas Weekly Herald printed the news on August 10 in its "Special to the Herald" letter from Lampasas, between notes on the harvest outlook and visitors to the town, and gave the motive as a supposition: "It is supposed that he was mobbed for horse stealing." Out-of-state papers carried a shorter wire version among "Condensed Telegrams" and similar columns, including the Bolivar Bulletin in Tennessee, the Burlington Weekly Free Press in Vermont, the Grenada Sentinel in Mississippi and the St. Landry Democrat in Louisiana.

The briefs ran without comment, but their wording differed. The South Kentuckian of Hopkinsville called Porter "a horse thief" outright and misprinted the town as "Larapasos," while the Burlington paper spelled it "Lampassas."

The size of the mob differs between versions: the Lampasas correspondent and most wire briefs gave about twenty-five men, while the Burlington Weekly Free Press reported "Seventy-five men." The local figure of twenty-five, from the earliest and closest report, is the better-supported one.

bases: A mob of twenty-five or more men took Porter from a cattle camp and shot him to death on suspicion of horse stealing (A1, A3, A4).
A mob of about twenty-five men (seventy-five in one brief) seized Porter and shot him dead without any legal process, reportedly because he had a horse supposed to be stolen (A1, A3, A4).

A Lampasas special to the Dallas Herald and a separate condensed-telegram wire version agree on the mob, the victim's name, the shooting and the horse-stealing suspicion, though the wire may derive from the Texas report (A1, A3, A4).
